method: S1 is the open RACGP AJGP 2024 dysmenorrhoea review, fetched and checked verbatim (29 claims, 3 of them dosing-regimen claims that are machine re-checkable). A1 is AMH, read under subscription and PARAPHRASED across the 'Dysmenorrhoea' and 'Premenstrual syndrome' topics (15 claims, 3 doses); no passage reproduced, no source_text stored. NO NSAID DOSE appears anywhere: S1 gives the TIMING of NSAID use precisely and names no drug or amount, and A1 gives neither. That gap is recorded rather than filled from memory or from the NSAID monograph, which was not retrieved. COC dosing for these indications lives in the contraception guideline, whose 1.1 edition retrieved that monograph on the same day; it is cross-linked, not duplicated.

claims.claim: Dysmenorrhoea is the most common gynaecologic condition affecting people assigned female at birth, with reported prevalence varying from 45% to 95% of all menstruating people and up to 93% of adolescents
claims.source_text: Dysmenorrhoea, defined as painful menstruation, is one of the most common gynaecologic conditions affecting adolescents, women and people assigned female at birth (AFAB) during their menstruating years. Reported prevalence varies from 45% to 95% of all menstruating people 1,2 and up to 93% of adolescents.

claims.claim: An Australian study of people assigned female at birth aged 16 to 29 found 88% reported dysmenorrhoea although only 34% had ever consulted a healthcare provider about period pain, while 86% had sought information from other sources such as the internet, social media, family or friends
claims.source_text: An Australian study of people AFAB aged 16 to 29 found that 88% reported dysmenorrhoea, although only 34% had ever consulted a healthcare provider about period pain. In contrast, 86% had sought information about period pain from other sources, such as the internet, social media, family or friends.

claims.claim: There can be cultural influences on reporting or seeking care due to the normalisation of menstrual pain, stigma, shame and misinformation, but rates appear consistent across cultures irrespective of geographic location, economic status of the country and ethnicity
claims.source_text: There can be cultural influences on reporting or seeking care due to the normalisation of menstrual pain, stigma, shame and misinformation, 2 but the rates do appear to be consistent across cultures irrespective of geographic location, economic status of the country and ethnicity.

claims.claim: Clinicians have a role in screening for dysmenorrhoea and recognising unique challenges in providing care safely for all patients including those living with disability, First Nations people, those with culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds and those who identify as transgender, non-binary, lesbian, intersex and queer
claims.source_text: Clinicians have a role to play in screening for dysmenorrhoea in their patients and recognising that there can be unique challenges in providing care in a safe way for all patients, including those living with disability, First Nations people, those with culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds and those who identify as transgender, non-binary, lesbian, intersex and queer.

claims.claim: Dysmenorrhoea is the leading cause of recurrent short-term school or work absenteeism among women of child-bearing age, with 20% reporting absences from school or university, 40% a negative effect on schoolwork or focus, 37% a reduction in other activities, and an estimated 10 to 30% of those working or studying losing one to two working days per month
claims.source_text: It is the leading cause of recurrent, short-term school or work absenteeism among women of child-bearing age. 7 According to De Sanctis et al, 20% of girls and women reported absences from school or university due to dysmenorrhoea, and 40% reported a negative effect on their schoolwork or focus. 2 Thirty-seven per cent reported a reduction in other activities, such as participation in social or sporting activities. 2 An estimated 10-30% of people with dysmenorrhoea who are working or studying lose one to two working days per month.

claims.claim: Dysmenorrhoea is classified as primary or secondary based on whether underlying pathology is found, with secondary dysmenorrhoea accounting for around 10% of cases
claims.source_text: Dysmenorrhoea is classified as primary or secondary based on whether underlying pathology is found, with secondary dysmenorrhoea accounting for around 10% of cases.

claims.claim: Primary dysmenorrhoea typically presents as crampy pelvic pain in the lower abdomen or pelvis occurring just before or during menstruation and lasting 8 to 72 hours, may radiate to the back or thighs, commonly has systemic symptoms including nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, fatigue, bloating and insomnia, and typically begins 6 to 12 months from menarche
claims.source_text: Primary dysmenorrhoea typically presents as crampy pelvic pain in the lower abdomen or pelvis, occurring just before and/or during menstruation and lasting 8-72 hours. 1,7 The pain might radiate to the back or thighs, and accompanying systemic symptoms are common, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, fatigue, bloating and insomnia. 1,7 Typical onset is 6-12 months from menarche.

claims.claim: Risk factors for primary dysmenorrhoea include smoking, menarche under 12 years, age under 30 years, longer and heavier menstrual flow, low or high body mass index, nulliparity, positive family history, previous sexual assault, premenstrual symptoms, previous pelvic inflammatory disease and psychological disorders, while protective factors include increasing age, increasing parity, exercise and oral contraceptive use
claims.source_text: Risk factors for primary dysmenorrhoea include smoking, menarche <12 years, age <30 years, longer and heavier menstrual flow, low or high body mass index (<20 or >30), nulliparity, positive family history, previous sexual assault, premenstrual symptoms, previous pelvic inflammatory disease and psychological disorders. 6,12,13 Protective factors include increasing age, increasing parity, exercise and oral contraceptive use.

claims.claim: The main mechanism appears to be uterine myometrial hypercontractility and vasoconstriction from elevated prostaglandins released by degenerating cells during endometrial sloughing, with prostaglandin F2 alpha thought to sensitise pain receptors directly and pain intensity proportional to the amount present
claims.source_text: The main mechanism of primary dysmenorrhoea, whether primary or secondary, appears to be uterine myometrial hypercontractility and vasoconstriction as a result of elevated levels of prostaglandins released by degenerating cells during endometrial sloughing. 1,7,13 Prostaglandin F2 (PGF 2α) and prostaglandin E2 (PGE 2) in particular appear to be important, and PGF 2α is thought to have a direct effect in sensitising pain receptors. There are elevated concentrations of PGF 2 α in the menstrual fluid of people with primary dysmenorrhoea, and the intensity of pain is proportional to the amount of PGF 2 α present.

claims.claim: The most common cause of secondary dysmenorrhoea is endometriosis, with other causes including Mullerian malformations, adenomyosis, leiomyomas, pelvic masses and infection
claims.source_text: Secondary dysmenorrhoea is menstrual pain attributed to pelvic pathology. 12 The most common aetiology is endometriosis, 7,12 but other aetiologies include congenital or acquired obstructive and non-obstructive abnormalities, such as Mullerian malformations, adenomyosis, leiomyomas, pelvic masses and infection.

claims.claim: Symptoms that should prompt consideration of secondary dysmenorrhoea include worsening pelvic pain, abnormal bleeding, vaginal discharge, dyspareunia and a lack of response to treatment such as NSAIDs or hormonal treatments
claims.source_text: Symptoms that should prompt consideration of secondary dysmenorrhoea include worsening pelvic pain, abnormal bleeding, vaginal discharge, dyspareunia and a lack of response to treatment such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatories (NSAIDs) or hormonal treatments.

claims.claim: There is a growing body of evidence supporting the role of central sensitisation in primary dysmenorrhoea, with high co-occurrence with or progression to other chronic pain conditions including irritable bowel syndrome, low back pain, interstitial cystitis, chronic pelvic and abdominal musculoskeletal pain, vulvodynia, fibromyalgia, chronic headache, temporomandibular joint disease and chronic fatigue syndrome
claims.source_text: There appears to be altered pain sensitivity in people with primary dysmenorrhoea, 1 and there is a growing body of evidence to support the role of central sensitisation in its aetiology. 7,16,17 There is a high co-occurrence with, or progression to, other chronic pain conditions, including irritable bowel syndrome, low back pain, interstitial cystitis/painful bladder syndrome, chronic pelvic and abdominal musculoskeletal pain, vulvodynia, fibromyalgia, chronic headache, temporomandibular joint disease and chronic fatigue syndrome.

claims.claim: Experimental studies have found alterations in central processing of noxious stimuli that persist when there is no background pain and in response to stimuli distant from the clinical pain, suggesting possible maladaptive functionality of pain modulatory systems making people with primary dysmenorrhoea vulnerable to functional pain disorders
claims.source_text: Experimental studies have found that there are alterations in the central processing of experimental noxious stimuli and that these alterations persist when there is no background pain and in response to stimuli at a distant site from that of the clinical pain. 20 This suggests possible maladaptive functionality of pain modulatory systems in people with primary dysmenorrhoea, making them vulnerable to functional pain disorders.

claims.claim: Pelvic examination is not routinely indicated if the history suggests primary dysmenorrhoea but should be performed along with pelvic ultrasound if there are features of secondary dysmenorrhoea, and pregnancy should be excluded in patients who are sexually active with consideration given to screening for infections
claims.source_text: Pelvic examination is not routinely indicated if the history suggests primary dysmenorrhoea but should be performed, along with a pelvic ultrasound, if there are features of secondary dysmenorrhoea. 10,12 Pregnancy should be excluded in patients who are sexually active and consideration given to screening for infections.

claims.claim: S1 states that both primary and secondary dysmenorrhoea are likely to respond to the same therapy, so initiation of treatment should not depend on establishing a diagnosis
claims.source_text: Both primary and secondary dysmenorrhoea are likely to respond to the same therapy, so initiation of treatment should not depend on establishing a diagnosis.

claims.claim: NSAIDs are considered first-line therapy for primary dysmenorrhoea and all currently available NSAIDs are of comparable efficacy and safety
claims.source_text: They are considered the first-line therapy for primary dysmenorrhoea. 10,12 All currently available NSAID drugs are of comparable efficacy and safety.

claims.claim: S1 advises that NSAIDs should be taken on a regular dosing regimen and ideally initiated 1 to 2 days before the onset of menses and continued in regular dosing intervals through the first 2 to 3 days of bleeding, correlating with the highest levels of prostaglandins
claims.source_text: NSAIDs should be taken on a regular dosing regimen and ideally should be initiated 1-2 days before the onset of menses and continued in regular dosing intervals through the first 2-3 days of bleeding, correlating with the highest levels of prostaglandins.

claims.claim: S1 reports that patients had lower pain scores using a regimen with a higher loading dose followed by a lower scheduled amount than a traditional same-dose regimen, that only one-third of young patients take their recommended daily dosage, and that up to 20% report minimal or no relief
claims.source_text: Patients reported lower pain scores when using a regimen with a higher loading dose followed by a lower scheduled amount over a traditional same-dose regimen. 21 Only one-third of young patients take their recommended daily dosage, highlighting the need for prescribers to emphasise the recommended dosing regimen. 1 Up to 20% of patients report minimal or no relief.

claims.claim: NSAID gastrointestinal side effects can be ameliorated by taking with food or switching to a COX-2 inhibitor
claims.source_text: NSAIDs can be associated with gastrointestinal side effects, which can be ameliorated by taking with food or switching to a COX-2 inhibitor.

claims.claim: Both combined and progesterone-only hormonal therapies can be used for dysmenorrhoea and should be offered to adolescent and adult patients not currently planning pregnancy unless contraindications exist
claims.source_text: Both combined and progesterone-only hormonal therapies can be used to treat dysmenorrhoea and should be offered to adolescent and adult patients with dysmenorrhoea who are not currently planning pregnancy unless contraindications exist.

claims.claim: Combined oral contraceptives are effective for treating dysmenorrhoea in up to 90% of patients, working by inhibiting ovulation and preventing endometrial proliferation which decreases prostaglandin, progesterone and vasopressin production, and continuous or extended use is recommended over cyclic use
claims.source_text: Combined oral contraceptives are effective for treating dysmenorrhoea in up to 90% of patients. 1 They work by inhibiting ovulation and preventing endometrial proliferation, which decreases prostaglandin, progesterone and vasopressin production. 1,7,9 Continuous or extended use of hormonal contraceptives is recommended over cyclic use.

claims.claim: Progesterone-only treatments including oral progestogens, etonogestrel implants, depot medroxyprogesterone and levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine systems can be effective, mostly working by inhibiting ovulation and inducing endometrial atrophy, with levonorgestrel intrauterine systems shown to improve both primary and secondary dysmenorrhoea and safe in nulliparous and adolescent patients, though irregular bleeding is common
claims.source_text: Progesterone-only hormonal treatments can also be effective treatments for dysmenorrhoea, including oral progestogens, etonogestrel implants, depot medroxyprogesterone acetate and levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine systems (LNG-IUS). 1,7,17 In most cases, they work by inhibiting ovulation and induce endometrial atrophy, which reduces menstrual bleeding. LNG-IUS have been shown to improve both primary and secondary dysmenorrhoea and are safe to use in nulliparous and adolescent patients. 17 Irregular bleeding is common with progesterone-only options.

claims.claim: Most supplements and medications evaluated for dysmenorrhoea either lack sufficient evidence of benefit or have unacceptable side effects, but evidence supports ginger as an effective treatment with the added benefit of anti-emetic properties
claims.source_text: Various supplements and medications have been evaluated for dysmenorrhoea. Most either lack sufficient evidence of benefit or have unacceptable side effects. 1,7,22 Ginger has a range of anti-inflammatory actions, including inhibition of cyclo-oxygenase and lipoxygenase activity. 23 Evidence supports that ginger can be an effective treatment for dysmenorrhoea and has the added benefit of anti-emetic properties.

claims.claim: S1 reports low-quality evidence that 45 to 60 minutes of exercise of any intensity three or more times per week provides a clinically significant reduction in menstrual pain
claims.source_text: There is low-quality evidence that 45-60 minutes of exercise of any intensity three or more times per week provides a clinically significant reduction in menstrual pain.

claims.claim: Local heat in the form of heated pads or patches increases blood flow and improves tissue oxygenation and has been shown to be comparable to ibuprofen for treating dysmenorrhoea and superior to paracetamol or no intervention
claims.source_text: Local heat, in the form of heated pads or patches, increases blood flow and improves tissue oxygenation; it has been shown to be comparable to ibuprofen for treating dysmenorrhoea and to be superior to paracetamol or no intervention.

claims.claim: High frequency transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation has been shown to be superior to placebo and is helpful in approximately 30% of cycles in people with severe dysmenorrhoea, with lower doses of NSAIDs required in the remaining cycles
claims.source_text: High frequency transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) has been shown to be superior to placebo for dysmenorrhoea and is helpful in approximately 30% of cycles in people with severe dysmenorrhoea, whereas lower doses of NSAIDs are required to manage pain in the remaining cycles.

claims.claim: There is low-quality data supporting acupuncture and acupressure which can be considered for those wishing to use complementary or alternative therapies, and almost all studies of physiotherapy have shown a significant improvement in pain intensity
claims.source_text: There is low-quality data supporting the effectiveness of acupuncture and acupressure, 27 and these therapies can be considered for those wishing to use complementary or alternative therapies. 10 Many studies have evaluated various types and methods of physiotherapy for dysmenorrhoea. 28 Overall, almost all studies of physiotherapy have shown a significant improvement in pain intensity among patients with dysmenorrhoea.

claims.claim: Surgical intervention should only be considered for primary dysmenorrhoea if a concerted trial of medical therapy has not been successful, with preoperative assessment to look for secondary causes including detailed history, clinical examination, pelvic ultrasound and possibly MRI
claims.source_text: Surgical intervention should only be considered for primary dysmenorrhoea if a concerted trial of medical therapy has not been successful. 10 Preoperative assessment should be undertaken to look for secondary causes and to direct appropriate therapy, including a detailed history and clinical examination, a pelvic ultrasound and possibly magnetic resonance imaging.

claims.claim: S1 states that dysmenorrhoea is frequently undertreated despite effective therapy being widely available at minimal cost, and that practitioners should consider screening for dysmenorrhoea at the time of other preventative health checks such as cervical screening
claims.source_text: Most patients will respond to interventions that can be initiated in a primary care setting, and yet dysmenorrhoea is frequently undertreated despite effective therapy being widely available at minimal cost. Patients should be encouraged to discuss their menstrual health with their general practitioner to improve uptake of treatment, and practitioners should consider screening for dysmenorrhoea at the time of other preventative health checks, such as cervical screening.
